headline: This law changes how the federal government stores, sells, and manages helium, and it also extends several unrelated federal programs for rural schools, parks, and mines.
what_it_does: The law directs the Interior Department to sell federal helium in phases, with auctions to qualified bidders that grow each year until all helium available is auctioned from fiscal year 2020 on, and it requires fees for storage, withdrawal, and transportation that cover the government's full costs. Money from helium sales and fees goes to a Helium Production Fund, and extra money is sent to the Treasury to help reduce the federal deficit. The law also sets a plan to dispose of federal helium facilities by September 30, 2021, funds research on helium recovery and separation, and extends several temporary programs, including rural school and road payments, abandoned well cleanup, national park maintenance cost-sharing, a cap change for mine reclamation payments, a temporary royalty rate for sodium compounds, and a reduction in an advanced biofuels grant authorization.

who_it_affects.group: Helium buyers, including medical, scientific, industrial, and commercial users
who_it_affects.how: They can buy crude helium from the federal reserve through sales and auctions, and the law sets the schedule and prices they will face.

They can bid in annual federal helium auctions and store purchased helium in the federal reserve, and refiners must make excess refining capacity available at commercially reasonable rates as a condition of purchase.

who_it_affects.group: Federal agencies and federal helium users
who_it_affects.how: They get priority access to the federal helium pipeline and reserve, and they are asked to plan for long-term helium supply and possible shortages.

who_it_affects.group: Counties and states with federal land
who_it_affects.how: Their payments for schools and roads are extended through fiscal year 2013 under the Secure Rural Schools Act.

who_it_affects.group: National Park Service visitors and park staff
who_it_affects.how: Parks can receive federal money for deferred maintenance projects, but at least half of each project's cost must come from non-federal sources.

who_it_affects.group: States and tribes that receive abandoned coal mine reclamation payments
who_it_affects.how: Their annual payment limits are waived for 2014 and 2015 but capped at set amounts for each year.

who_it_affects.group: Producers of sodium compounds on federal land
who_it_affects.how: Their royalty rate is set at 4 percent for two years after enactment.

who_it_affects.group: Natural gas producers and helium researchers
who_it_affects.how: The Energy Department will fund programs to capture helium from natural gas streams and reduce helium venting during gas operations.

when_it_takes_effect: The law was signed October 2, 2013, and many provisions began then, while others have later dates such as a one-time helium sale by August 1, 2014, the end of Phase A on October 1, 2014, and the disposal phase ending September 30, 2021.
